The High Court held that the levy could be justified only if the property tax was leviable on the basis of annual letting value of the house, building or land called property tax. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the levy. The High court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The levy of property taxes is a legislative function. The legislature has no power to impose a tax on the entry of goods into a local area for consumption, use or sale therein. The entry does not confer any power upon the State to impose a particular tax. The entry is subject to the legislative competence of the legislature which enacted it. [9 G] (2) The State Legislature can impose a tax either on the entry or on the entry. The State Legislature cannot impose a tax directly on the entry itself. [10 D] (3) The State legislature can impose a rate on the entry tax on the basis on annual letting value. [11 E] (4) The State Government can impose a general tax on the taxable event. [12 F] (5) The State is empowered to impose a general rate on the taxable events. The State can impose a special rate on the basis only of the annual letting value or the annual letting values of the property. [13 C] (6) The State can also impose a general levy on the basis or basis of the annual rental value of the property in question. [14 D]
784: The appellant was granted a lease of the slate quarries and other ancillary reliefs in the year 1945. He applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease, but he refused to do so on the ground that the lease had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945, and that, as the lease was for a period exceeding one year, it was not enforceable against the Government by the operation of the body of sub section (1) itself. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order passed by the Board of Revenue. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the lease could be terminated only under the third proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The first proviso to section 10(2)(a) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, which provides for compensation for termination of the lease is not applicable to the case before us. [880 B] (ii) The second proviso to section 40(1) does not apply to the case where the lease has been granted prior to July 1. 1945. It applies only to cases where the lease is for a period not exceeding one year. The second proviso does not apply where the lease was granted after July 1, 1946. [881 C] (iii)The second proviso to sub section (2) of section 20 of the Abolition of Act is not attracted because the lease was not for a period of less than one year. [882 D] (iv)The second part of the proviso to section 30(1) is not applicable because the lease had already been granted prior thereto. [883 F] (v)The second limb of the proviso is not applicable since the lease was given prior to July, 1945. [884 G] (vi)In the instant case, the lease was executed on July 1, 1944, and the lease was renewed from time to time. The appellant did not challenge the validity of sub section 2 of section 20 read with section 40(2) of the Act. [885 A] (vii)The second condition of sub section 3 of section 20 is not satisfied because the lease is governed by the third proviso. [886 B]
